# Accessibility {.unnumbered} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [Caution]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} This section is being revised. Thank you for your patience. ::: :::: How do we reach RStudio Server, JupyterHub, and `baseball-trajectory` on the same instance without opening a port for each one? The answer from [Lab 12](lab12.qmd) is a proxy. In this chapter we install the two new services, keep every port but `80` closed to the outside, and put `nginx` in front. RStudio Server lives at `/rstudio`, JupyterHub at `/jupyter`, and the app from [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd) at `/trajectory`. ## What we're building Only port `80` opens in the security group. `nginx` listens there and reads the path of each request. It forwards `/rstudio/` to RStudio Server on `8787`, `/jupyter/` to JupyterHub on `8001`, and `/trajectory/` to the app on `8000`. Everything else gets the `nginx` welcome page: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'One Port, Four Destinations' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD Browser(["Browser"]) SG{"Security group
port 80 from our IP"} subgraph Instance["EC2 instance"] Nginx("nginx

127.0.0.1:8000") end Browser --> SG --> Nginx Nginx --"/"--> Welcome Nginx --"/rstudio/"--> RS Nginx --"/jupyter/"--> JH Nginx --"/trajectory/"--> App style Browser fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 style SG fill:#D2562B,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Nginx fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Welcome fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style RS fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style JH fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style App fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff ``` `baseball-trajectory` already holds `8000`, and JupyterHub uses `8000` by default. JupyterHub moves to `8001` so both can run. In [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd#viewing-the-app) only we could see the app, through an SSH tunnel; here anyone the security group allows can reach it. [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd) later moves it to `443`. ## Logging into the instance We use the same AL2023 instance from [Instance Size](instance-size.qmd). It already has R 4.6.1 (from `rig`) and Python 3.12.1 in `/opt`. Start it, look up the new IP, and connect the same way as in [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd#logging-into-the-instance), or with `awsdev` from [SSH config](ssh-config.qmd). The instance is a `t3.small`, which we kept for this chapter (see [Staying on a `t3.small`](instance-size.qmd#staying-on-a-t3.small)). RStudio Server and JupyterHub add two more services that need memory, so check what's free before we start: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} free -h ``` ::: ## A user to log in with RStudio Server and JupyterHub both log users in with their Linux username and password. `ec2-user` has no password (we log in with a key), so create a user for the lab and give it one: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo useradd -m datasci sudo passwd datasci ``` ::: `-m` creates `/home/datasci`, which both services need for the user's files and sessions. ## Installing RStudio Server Posit doesn't build RStudio Server for Amazon Linux. We use the RHEL 9 package, for the same reason `rig` could use the RHEL 9 build of R: AL2023 is close enough to RHEL 9. Copy the current RHEL 9 download link from the [RStudio Server download page](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-server/) and download it: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} cd /tmp curl -LO https://download2.rstudio.org/server/rhel9/x86_64/rstudio-server-rhel-VERSION-x86_64.rpm ``` ::: `dnf` installs the package and the libraries it depends on: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo dnf install -y ./rstudio-server-rhel-VERSION-x86_64.rpm ``` ::: The package installs a `systemd` unit and starts it. Check that it's running: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo systemctl status rstudio-server ``` ::: ### Keeping RStudio Server private RStudio Server listens on every address by default. We want it reachable only through `nginx`, the same way `baseball-trajectory` binds to `127.0.0.1`. Open its config file: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo vim /etc/rstudio/rserver.conf ``` ::: Add one line: ```{.default} www-address=127.0.0.1 ``` Restart RStudio Server to load the change: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo systemctl restart rstudio-server ``` ::: We could also set `www-root-path=/rstudio` here. We don't need to, because `nginx` sends the same information in a header (see below). ## Installing JupyterHub JupyterHub has two parts. The hub logs users in and starts a notebook server for each one. `configurable-http-proxy`, a Node.js program, sits in front and routes each user's traffic to their server. That means JupyterHub needs Node.js as well as Python: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo dnf install -y nodejs npm sudo npm install -g configurable-http-proxy ``` ::: `npm install -g` puts the proxy in `/usr/local/bin`. Check that it's on the `PATH`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} which configurable-http-proxy ``` ::: The Python side gets its own virtual environment in `/opt`, built from the `/opt` Python just like `baseball-trajectory`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 -m venv /opt/jupyterhub/.venv sudo /opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/pip install jupyterhub jupyterlab ``` ::: ### Configuring JupyterHub JupyterHub writes a default config file that lists every setting, all commented out. Generate it in `/etc/jupyterhub`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo mkdir -p /etc/jupyterhub cd /etc/jupyterhub sudo /opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/jupyterhub --generate-config ``` ::: Open the file and add three settings at the top: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo vim /etc/jupyterhub/jupyterhub_config.py ``` ::: ```{.default} c.JupyterHub.bind_url = 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/jupyter' #<1> c.Spawner.cmd = ['/opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/jupyterhub-singleuser'] #<2> c.Spawner.default_url = '/lab' #<3> ``` 1. The address, port, and path JupyterHub serves from. `127.0.0.1` keeps it private, `8001` avoids `baseball-trajectory`, and `/jupyter` matches the path in `nginx`. 2. The program that starts each user's notebook server, with its full path into the venv. 3. Users land in JupyterLab instead of the classic notebook page. The path in `bind_url` is the setting the chapter warns about. JupyterHub writes its links relative to that path. Without `/jupyter`, the login page loads but every link on it points at `/` and gets the `nginx` welcome page instead. ### Running JupyterHub as a service JupyterHub doesn't ship a unit file, so we write one, the same way we did for `baseball-trajectory` in [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd#the-unit-file): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo vim /etc/systemd/system/jupyterhub.service ``` ::: ```{.default} [Unit] Description=JupyterHub After=network.target [Service] User=root #<1> Environment="PATH=/opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin" #<2> WorkingDirectory=/etc/jupyterhub #<3> ExecStart=/opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/jupyterhub -f /etc/jupyterhub/jupyterhub_config.py Restart=on-failure [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target ``` 1. The hub runs as `root` because it has to start each user's server as that user. This is the opposite of `baseball-trajectory`, which runs as its own service account. 2. The `PATH` has to include `/usr/local/bin`, or the hub can't find `configurable-http-proxy`. 3. The hub writes its cookie secret and user database here. Load the unit, then enable and start it: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now jupyterhub sudo systemctl status jupyterhub ``` ::: ## Configuring nginx AL2023's `nginx` package already has a `server` block for port `80` in `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`. It serves the welcome page, and it reads any file in `/etc/nginx/default.d/`. That means we don't have to replace `nginx.conf`, as the chapter does on Ubuntu. We add two small files instead. Install `nginx` first: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo dnf install -y nginx ``` ::: Confirm the default `server` block includes `default.d`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} grep -n 'listen\|default.d' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf ``` ::: ### The WebSocket map RStudio and JupyterLab both keep a WebSocket open to the browser (see [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd)). `nginx` only passes it through when the request asks for an upgrade. A `map` sets that header for us, and it has to live in the `http` block, which reads every file in `conf.d/`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo vim /etc/nginx/conf.d/websocket.conf ``` ::: ```{.default} map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade; '' close; } ``` ### The three locations The `location` blocks go in `default.d/`, so they join the existing port `80` server: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo vim /etc/nginx/default.d/lab12.conf ``` ::: ```{.default} location /rstudio/ { rewrite ^/rstudio/(.*)$ /$1 break; #<1> proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade; proxy_read_timeout 20d; #<2> proxy_set_header X-RStudio-Root-Path /rstudio; #<3> proxy_set_header Host $host:$server_port; } location /jupyter/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8001; #<4> proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade; } location /trajectory/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000/; #<5> proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade; proxy_set_header Host $host; } ``` 1. RStudio Server expects paths that start at `/`, so `nginx` strips `/rstudio` before passing the request on. 2. Keeps an idle RStudio session's connection open instead of dropping it after 60 seconds. 3. Tells RStudio Server it lives at `/rstudio`, so the links it writes include the prefix. 4. No `rewrite` here. JupyterHub already serves from `/jupyter` (its `bind_url`), so the path passes through unchanged. 5. The trailing `/` on `proxy_pass` strips `/trajectory/` before the request reaches the app. The app thinks it lives at `/`, and it works because Shiny writes its links relative to the page. Each service handles the path its own way. RStudio Server gets the prefix stripped and a header telling it where it lives. JupyterHub keeps the prefix because its own config already expects it. `baseball-trajectory` gets the prefix stripped and needs nothing else, so its unit file stays as it is. ### Testing and starting nginx `nginx -t` checks every file for errors before we start the server: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo nginx -t ``` ::: Enable and start `nginx`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo systemctl enable --now nginx ``` ::: `ss` shows every service and the address it listens on. Only `nginx` should listen on all addresses (`0.0.0.0:80`); the rest stay on `127.0.0.1`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo ss -tlnp ``` ::: Before touching the security group, test all three paths from the instance itself. `curl -I` asks for the headers only: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} curl -I http://127.0.0.1/rstudio/ curl -I http://127.0.0.1/jupyter/ curl -I http://127.0.0.1/trajectory/ ``` ::: A `302` is a good sign for the first two. RStudio Server and JupyterHub redirect a visitor who isn't logged in to their sign in page. The app has no login, so it should answer `200 OK`, the same as the `curl -I` in [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd). ## Opening port 80 From outside, the request still hangs. The security group only allows port `22`. Add a rule for port `80` from our local machine: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \ --group-name dev-sg \ --protocol tcp --port 80 \ --cidr YOUR_IP/32 \ --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: The chapter opens port `80` to everyone (`0.0.0.0/0`). We limit it to our own IP, the same as the SSH rule. This site is plain HTTP, so the `datasci` password crosses the internet unencrypted until [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd) adds HTTPS. ## Trying it out Open `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/` in a browser. The `nginx` welcome page confirms the proxy and the security group work. Then try each path: * `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/rstudio/`: RStudio Server's sign in page. Sign in as `datasci`. * `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/jupyter/`: JupyterHub's login page. Sign in as `datasci`, and JupyterLab opens. * `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/trajectory/`: `baseball-trajectory`, with no SSH tunnel this time. Type `http://` in full. Some browsers try `https://` first, and nothing listens on `443` yet. Keep the trailing `/` too, since each `location` block matches a path that ends in `/`. With both sessions open, check memory again: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} free -h ``` ::: ## Recap 1. One open port can serve several services, including the app we could only reach through an SSH tunnel before. `nginx` listens on `80` and sends each path to a service that only listens on `127.0.0.1`. 2. Each service needs to know its path. RStudio Server learns it from the `X-RStudio-Root-Path` header, and JupyterHub learns it from `bind_url`. `baseball-trajectory` never needs to know, because `nginx` strips the prefix and Shiny's links are relative. 3. On AL2023, the `location` blocks go in `/etc/nginx/default.d/` and the WebSocket `map` goes in `/etc/nginx/conf.d/`, so `nginx.conf` stays untouched. 4. The new security group rule opens port `80` to our IP only, because plain HTTP sends passwords unencrypted. [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd) adds HTTPS.
